## Where This Fits
This week supplies the *input-side language* that every later module speaks. For students with no prior background it is the only systematic pass through DSP in the whole semester, and the only systematic pass through phonetics, so it is kept deliberately narrow: only what will be used later. On the signal side that means sampling, the STFT, mel, phase, F0 and SNR — not filter design in general. On the phonetics side it means phones versus phonemes, how consonants are articulated, coarticulation, and the three acoustic correlates of prosody (F0, duration, energy).

That last item matters more in this course than in most. Mandarin, Taiwanese Hokkien and Hakka are tone languages: F0 carries lexical content and intonation on the same curve. The consequences come back repeatedly — when we tokenise speech (W6), when we try to control synthesis (W9), and when we look for turn-taking cues (W12).

## Learning Objectives
1. Derive the time–frequency resolution trade-off of the STFT, and keep apart three quantities that are routinely conflated: window length sets frequency resolution and lookahead, hop sets the frame rate, and the FFT size only sets the bin spacing.
2. Explain how the source–filter model separates the excitation (F0, voicing) from the vocal-tract filter (formants, spectral envelope) in the frequency domain, and say where that separation breaks — including why "source = who is speaking, filter = what is said" does not hold in a tone language.
3. Motivate each step of log-mel and MFCC (why the log, why mel, why the DCT), explain why MFCC has largely given way to log-mel in the deep-learning era, and point out where two implementations of "log-mel" can differ.
4. Split the distortion of "waveform from spectrogram" into its three sources — phase, mel compression, and over-smoothed predicted spectra — and use STFT consistency to explain why Griffin-Lim is possible and why it is not enough.
5. List the three acoustic correlates of prosody, explain how lexical tone and intonation share F0, and predict what that implies for methods developed mainly on English: semantic tokens, prosody control, and prosodic turn-taking cues.

## Demos
Two of this week's three demos are programs; they are published so that you can read them, re-run them, and change them — **you are not required to run anything**. Each folder's `README.md` gives requirements, setup, commands, and what you should see; the index at [`demos/`](https://github.com/hungshinlee/Speech-AI/tree/main/demos) explains the shared environment.

| | Slides | What it shows | Needs | Runs on |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [Demo 1 · live spectrogram, pitch track, vowel chart](https://github.com/hungshinlee/Speech-AI/tree/main/demos/w02_d1_spectrogram) | p12, p23, p52 | A microphone, a 4 s scrolling spectrogram switchable between a 5 ms and a 30 ms window, an autocorrelation $F_0$ track, and an LPC $(F_1, F_2)$ dot on a vowel chart. Used three times: vowels /a/ /i/ /u/ and the glide between them; freeze and switch window length on the *same* sound (striations vs. harmonics); Mandarin tones and then a question. Set the pitch ceiling too low and watch the octave error. A Praat script for exact readings is included | `numpy` + `scipy` + `matplotlib` + `sounddevice`, a microphone; all DSP in `demos/dsp.py` | any laptop |
| [Demo 2 · phase × magnitude: the 2 × 3 reconstruction grid](https://github.com/hungshinlee/Speech-AI/tree/main/demos/w02_d2_phase_mel) | p34, p40, p42 | One sentence re-synthesised with linear or mel-80 magnitude crossed with original, Griffin-Lim or random phase, plus mel-40/20/10 with the original phase, so each distortion can be heard alone. Rehearsal: Griffin-Lim brings the log-spectral distance from 8.47 dB (random phase) to 1.71 dB at 256 iterations while the waveform SNR stays between −1 and −4 dB; with mel-80 in the chain the LSD floors near 6 dB. The ISTFT is the least-squares one, Griffin-Lim is the 1984 original without momentum, `librosa` is deliberately not used | `numpy` + `scipy` + `matplotlib`; the lecturer's recording and its reconstructions are not published — record your own 5 s sentence | any laptop |
| Demo 3 · front-end mismatch | p58 | Not built: same audio, same pretrained recogniser, only the mel recipe changed (HTK vs. Slaney, filterbank normalisation on or off), WER compared. The slide presents it as an experiment not yet run | — | — |

Tested on one machine only — an Apple M5 Max (64 GB, no CUDA), macOS 26.6, Python 3.12 — with the versions pinned in `demos/versions.lock`. Menus and labels are in Chinese; the keys are listed in each README.

## References
- **JM3** Ch 15 *Phonetics and Speech Feature Extraction* — the reference for both halves of the week, phonetics and feature extraction
- **HAH** Ch 2 (Spoken Language Structure), Ch 5 (Digital Signal Processing), Ch 6 (Speech Signal Representations) — the full derivations of the cepstrum, LPC and the source–filter model are here
- Griffin & Lim, **Signal Estimation from Modified Short-Time Fourier Transform**, IEEE TASSP, 1984
- Nawab, Quatieri & Lim, **Signal Reconstruction from Short-Time Fourier Transform Magnitude**, IEEE TASSP 31(4):986–998, 1983 — the conditions under which the STFT magnitude alone determines the signal
- Davis & Mermelstein, **Comparison of Parametric Representations for Monosyllabic Word Recognition in Continuously Spoken Sentences**, IEEE TASSP 28(4):357–366, 1980 — the original MFCC paper
- Stevens, Volkmann & Newman, **A Scale for the Measurement of the Psychological Magnitude Pitch**, JASA 8(3):185–190, 1937 — where the mel scale comes from. Read it to see that mel is the outcome of a small perceptual experiment, not a physical quantity
- de Cheveigné & Kawahara, **YIN, a Fundamental Frequency Estimator for Speech and Music**, JASA 111(4):1917–1930, 2002
- Mauch & Dixon, **pYIN: A Fundamental Frequency Estimator Using Probabilistic Threshold Distributions**, ICASSP 2014
- Kim, Salamon, Li & Bello, **CREPE: A Convolutional Representation for Pitch Estimation**, ICASSP 2018
- F0 modelling in tone languages (further searching): *tone sandhi Taiwanese Southern Min acoustic*, *lexical tone discrete speech units*, *tonal language self-supervised speech representation tone*, *tone intonation interaction F0*
- SI-SDR, definition and motivation: *SDR half-baked or well done* (used formally in W10)
- LPC meets neural networks: *LPCNet linear prediction neural vocoder*
- Front-ends and deep learning: *learnable filterbank speech*, *SincNet*, *LEAF frontend learnable audio*
